subject: Chemistry
title: Nanomedicine: Tiny Drug Carriers
description: A 60-second lesson on Nanomedicine: Tiny Drug Carriers.

hook.text: Nanoparticles can deliver drugs directly to cancer cells, sparing healthy tissue. The particles are smaller than a red blood cell.

buildup.text: Liposomes are hollow fat spheres 100 nm across. They encapsulate drugs, protecting them until they reach the target.

discovery.text: Tumors have leaky blood vessels with gaps that nanoparticles slip through. Healthy tissue has tight vessels that block them.

twist.text: Doxil was the first FDA-approved nanomedicine in 1995. It wraps toxic doxorubicin in liposomes to cut side effects.

climax.text: COVID mRNA vaccines use lipid nanoparticles to deliver mRNA into cells. The pandemic proved nanomedicine works at global scale.

punchline.text: Tiny fat spheres carrying medicine to precise targets. Drug delivery, revolutionized.

quiz.question: Why do nanoparticles accumulate in tumors but not healthy tissue?
options: Tumors have leaky blood vessels with gaps that nanoparticles can slip through
Nanoparticles are attracted to cancer cells by magnetic fields
Cancer cells actively absorb nanoparticles as food

details.summary: Nanomedicine uses nanoparticles between 1 and 100 nanometers to deliver drugs directly to diseased tissues while minimizing exposure to healthy organs..
details.whyItMatters: Nanoparticle drug delivery reduces side effects and improves efficacy by concentrating medicines at disease sites. The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines used lipid nanoparticles, demonstrating this technology at global scale.
takeaways: Nanoparticles can deliver drugs selectively to diseased tissue
The EPR effect causes nanoparticles to accumulate in leaky tumor vessels
COVID-19 mRNA vaccines validated lipid nanoparticle delivery at scale

faq.question: How do nanoparticles find and accumulate in tumor tissue?
faq.answer: Tumors grow rapidly and develop leaky blood vessels with gaps up to 800 nanometers wide. Nanoparticles are small enough to escape through these gaps but too large to leak back out through normal blood vessels. This passive accumulation, called the EPR effect, concentrates drugs in tumors.

faq.question: What are the main challenges preventing wider use of nanomedicine?
faq.answer: Manufacturing consistent nanoparticle populations at scale remains difficult and expensive. The immune system can recognize and clear nanoparticles before they reach their target. The EPR effect varies greatly between patients and tumor types, making efficacy unpredictable in clinical settings.
